Direct‐acting (also called instantaneous or on-demand) electric radiators convert virtually 100 percent of the electrical energy they draw into heat at the point of use. In that narrow sense—“from plug to radiator”—they are highly efficient. However, whether they make sense from an overall energy-and-cost perspective depends on several factors:

1. Energy source and supply  
   • If your electricity comes from fossil-fuelled generation (coal, oil or natural gas), the upstream losses in production and transmission can be substantial.  
   • In regions where the grid mix is dominated by renewables or nuclear, direct electric heating becomes more attractive from a carbon-emission standpoint.

2. Operating costs  
   • Electricity is almost always more expensive per kilowatt-hour than district heating, natural gas or heat-pump‐produced heat.  
   • Running direct electric radiators as a main heat source in a cold climate can lead to very high winter electricity bills.  

3. Usage pattern

Here are several practical measures you can take to get the most comfort and lowest running-costs from direct-acting electric radiators:

1. Install Fine-Control Thermostats and Timers  
   • Use individual room thermostats or thermostatic radiator valves (TRVs) so each heater only delivers the temperature you really need.  
   • Fit a weekly/daily timer or programmable thermostat to automatically reduce temperatures at night or when the house is empty. Even cutting back by 1 °C can save roughly 5 %–7 % on your heating bill.  

2. Zone Your Heating  
   • Divide your home into heating zones (e.g. living areas, bedrooms, bathrooms) so you only heat occupied rooms.  
   • Switch off or set to “frost protection” the radiators in seldom-used spaces.  

3. Maximise Building Insulation and Draught-Proofing  
   • Ensure windows and external doors are properly sealed—use draught strips or silicone caulk.  
   • Insulate lofts and cavity walls, and consider secondary glazing or low-emissivity

• AC charging (on-board)  
  – Slow charge: single-phase, up to 3.7 kW (often home wall-boxes)  
  – Fast charge: three-phase, 7–22 kW (public and workplace chargers)  

• DC charging (off-board, “rapid” or “fast”)  
  – From about 22–50 kW you’ll see smaller rapid chargers  
  – Above 50 kW is widely considered “DC fast charging” (often 50–350 kW ultra-rapid)

So if you’re comparing purely by charger power:  
– Anything up to 22 kW (AC) is “normal” or “fast AC.”  
– Once you go above 22 kW (and switch to DC), you’re in the “fast/rapid charging” category, with 50 kW+ DC considered true fast charging.

In Swedish practice stairwells are treated as “circulation spaces” rather than living rooms, and must be kept frost-free and reasonably comfortable. According to Boverket’s Building Regulations (BBR):

• Heated stairwells (part of the conditioned floor area Atemp) should be maintained at a minimum of 15 °C.  
• In many installations the set‐point is 15–18 °C to avoid cold drafts and surface condensation.  
• If a stairwell is officially unconditioned (outside Atemp), it only needs frost protection—typically around 10 °C.

There is no specific EPC (energideklaration) field for stairwell temperature; instead you follow the current BBR requirements, with 15 °C as the commonly cited minimum for heated circulation areas.
